abstract: {beta}-Carbolines are bioactive indole alkaloids with remarkable pharmacological properties and a defining role in ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian shamanic brew, where their inhibition of monoamine oxidases enables the oral activity of the psychoactive N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT). Yet, despite their longstanding medicinal and cultural significance, the biosynthetic origin of {beta}-carbolines in plants remains largely unresolved. Here, we uncover key steps underlying the biosynthesis of harmine, the major bioactive {beta}-carboline alkaloid in Peganum harmala, by integrating spatial metabolite and transcriptome profiling with enzyme characterization and pathway reconstruction. We discovered four enzymes that enable de novo harmine biosynthesis in Nicotiana benthamiana and revealed how two closely related cytochrome P450s exhibit divergent regioselectivity, directing tryptamine towards either {beta}-carboline or serotonin biosynthesis. Structural modeling and targeted mutagenesis pinpoint active-site residues that switch this regioselectivity, revealing a molecular basis for diversification of tryptamine metabolism. By combining distinct tryptamine pathways, we achieved de novo co-production of {beta}-carbolines and DMT in N. benthamiana and P. harmala hairy roots without supplementing exogenous precursors. Together, these findings unlock {beta}-carboline biosynthesis for future sustainable bioproduction with broad opportunities spanning medicine, crop protection, and biodiversity conservation.
